what_its_for: This combination medicine is used to help control blood sugar (glucose) levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works in two ways: empagliflozin helps your kidneys remove extra sugar from your body through your urine, while metformin reduces the amount of sugar your liver makes and helps your body use insulin more effectively. It is used along with diet and exercise to manage your blood sugar.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with food, preferably with a meal, to help reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, chew, or split it unless your doctor says it is okay (especially for extended-release tablets). Drink plenty of water throughout the day while taking this medicine. Take it at the same time(s) each day to help you remember.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take and how often. The usual starting dose is one tablet taken twice a day with meals for the immediate-release form, or once daily with the evening meal for the extended-release form. Your doctor may adjust your dose over time based on your blood sugar levels and how well you tolerate the medicine. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still close to the time you normally take it. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store this medicine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in a dry place, away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed and keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis (a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in the blood) and can also affect your blood sugar levels. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink enough fluids each day, especially in hot weather or during exercise. Tell your doctor before having any X-ray or scan that requires an injectable dye (contrast agent), as you may need to temporarily stop this medicine. Avoid skipping meals, as this could lead to low blood sugar, especially if you also take insulin or other diabetes medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, feeling cold, or feeling dizzy or lightheaded (these could be signs of lactic acidosis). Also contact your doctor if you notice: signs of a urinary tract infection (burning when urinating, frequent urination, or pelvic pain); pain or tenderness around your genitals or inner thighs (could be a rare but serious infection); signs of a yeast infection (itching, discharge, or unusual smell in the genital area); signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, confusion, or hunger); signs of a severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing); or if you are about to have surgery or a medical procedure.
when_it_works: Metformin starts working within the first few days, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks to see a noticeable change in your blood sugar levels. Empagliflozin can begin lowering blood sugar within the first day or two. However, it may take several weeks of consistent use, along with healthy eating and exercise, before you see the full benefit of this combination medicine. Keep taking it as directed even if you feel well, because type 2 diabetes often has no symptoms.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Use with caution, as older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as dehydration, low blood pressure, and kidney problems. Your doctor may check your kidney function more often. Kidney problems: This medicine is not recommended if your kidneys are not working well. Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. Liver problems: This medicine should generally be avoided if you have significant liver disease. Pregnancy: This medicine is not recommended during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor right away if you become pregnant or are planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children under 18 years of age.
